Thailand bans new Routledge textbook on contemporary politics, citing national security threats
The Thai police have ordered a ban on the second edition of the Routledge Handbook of Contemporary Thailand, claiming that it contains chapters that could affect national security or cause unrest.
Edited by exiled academic Pavin Chachavalpongpun, the book contains chapters on the Thai military, the monarchy, and the use of the royal defamation law, as well as chapters on popular movements and other social and political issues. Pavin posted on Facebook on Thursday (5 November) that the book was banned for its content about the monarchy.
In a previous post, he wrote that book banning doesn’t work in the age of the internet, since people can buy e-books instead of hard copies. He also wrote that the ban would help promote the book.
Under the 2007 Printing Recordation Act, importing the book for distribution carries a prison sentence of up to three years, or a fine of up to 60,000 baht, or both. The police may also seize and destroy the book.
This is the second time one of Pavin’s publications has been banned in Thailand. In July 2023, the Thai authorities ordered a ban on his book “Rama X: The Thai Monarchy under King Vajiralongkorn” even before it was released.
iLaw noted that the police have banned six books since the Printing Recordation Act came into effect, all of which concerns the monarchy. Other than the two books by Pavin, the list includes:
Thailand’s Crisis and the Fight for Democracy by Giles Ungpakorn A Kingdom in Crisis by Andrew McGregor Marshall The November 2015 issue of the French edition of Marie Claire magazine The article “Thailand: Colossally Popular,” published in The New Age of the Kings: Modern Monarchies in Malaysia and the World

The Criminal Court has concluded hearings in the defamation case filed against Prachatai by the company that produced the “2475 Dawn of Revolution” Animation. The verdict is scheduled to be delivered on 25 November.

The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) has issued a statement condemning the sentencing of human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to an additional 2 years and 8 months in prison on a royal defamation charge and calls for the unconditional and immediate release of Anon and other prisoners of conscience. On 30 October Anon and four other activists were found guilty of royal defamation over speeches given at a protest on 25 November 2020 and sentenced to 2 years and 8 months in prison. The full statement reads: HRF strongly condemns the Thai court’s sentencing of human rights lawyer Anon Nampa to an additional two years and eight months in prison under the country’s royal defamation law (Article 112 of the Criminal Code) for criticizing the monarchy, bringing his total prison sentence to more than 34 years.
Anon is among more than 290 people who have been charged under the royal defamation law since the youth-led protests that began in 2020. He was among the first prominent figures to publicly challenge the longstanding taboo surrounding discussion of the monarchy in Thai https://ow.ly/cc6p5103VJq
The Thai regime has increasingly weaponized the royal defamation law to suppress freedom of dissent. Dozens remain detained, while others have been forced into exile. According to HRF's Tyranny Tracker, Thailand is ruled by a hybrid authoritarian regime, with civic space continuing to shrink. https://ow.ly/gifF5103VJp

Thai authorities should not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China, where they face grave risks of torture and other serious abuses, Human Rights Watch said today (4 November). The two Uyghur men have been detained by Thai authorities since 2014, when one of them was only 14 years old. They were serving a prison sentence for offenses related to an escape attempt from immigration detention in January 2020. On October 21, 2026, the authorities transferred them from Bangkok Central Prison to the Bangkok Immigration Detention Center Suan Phlu after they had served most of their seven-year sentence. Thai Foreign Ministry officials told a parliamentary committee that in August the Chinese embassy in Bangkok demanded their return to China.
Under Thai immigration law and regulations, the two Uyghur men will be deported to China unless they object to the deportation and are resettled to a third country. International Court of Justice to rule on 19 November in Myanmar Genocide case
The International Court of Justice has announced that it will deliver its judgment on November 19, 2026, in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Genocide Convention, Human Rights Watch said today in releasing a question-and-answer document on key issues in the case.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the International Court of Justice alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. This is not a criminal case against individuals, but a request for a legal determination of Myanmar’s state responsibility for genocide.
“The International Court of Justice’s Myanmar judgment will mark a crucial moment in the Rohingya’s quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling will also be a stark reminder that the oppression of the Rohingya is ongoing, and that rights-respecting countries need to act decisively to support them, promote justice for atrocities, and ensure their safe and voluntary return.”
The judgment, which is final with no possibility to appeal, will conclude the proceedings in this case before the court.

Gathering marks 20th anniversary of anti-coup suicide
Photo: Ginger Cat
On Saturday (31 October), a gathering took place at an overpass on Vibhavadi Road to mark the 20th anniversary of the death of Nuamthong Praiwan, a taxi driver who crashed his taxi into a tank and later took his own life in protest of the 19 September 2006 military coup.
Activists, politicians, and members of the public participated in the gathering, which started at around 12.30 with live music, followed by a Buddhist merit-making ceremony. Flowers were placed around the overpass.
The rapper Elevenfinger also performed at the gathering. Before the event ended, former Red Shirt leader Thida Tavornseth led the participants in making a pledge to push for a new Constitution in line with the result of the 2026 referendum and for the repeal of laws that are relics of military coups.
After the coup, on 30 September 2006, Nuamthong crashed his taxi into a tank parked near the Equestrian Statue of King Chulalongkorn to protest the coup. He was seriously injured..
On 31 October 2006, Nuamthong was found hanging from the overpass in front of the Thairath newspaper office on Vibhavadi Road. He had committed suicide after Akkara Thairoj, a deputy spokesperson for the military junta, expressed scepticism about his intentions by asserting that “nobody’s ideals are so great that they would sacrifice their lives for them.”
Nuamthong’s suicide note says that he voluntarily crashed his taxi and took his own life and that he dies to demand democracy, and that his suicide is also a response to Akkara’s insult. He also wrote that “I hope that in my next life, there shall be no more coups.”

Thailand must not return detained Uyghur refugees to China, say rights groups
A network of human rights organizations have called on the Thai government not to forcibly return two detained Uyghur refugees to China and to facilitate their resettlement in a third country.
In a joint statement, the Coalition for the Rights of Refugees and Stateless Persons (CRSP), Migrant Working Group (MWG) and Thailand Migration Reform Consortium (TMR) raised concerns about potential forced return to China of two Uyghur refugees detained at the Suan Phlu Immigration Dentetion Centre. The groups said that the two refugees have been detained since 2014 and were moved to immigration detention from prison on 21 October. They have told their legal representatives they do not consent to return to China, but their representatives have not been allowed to see them since their transfer.
The groups noted that, days after the two were moved to immigration detention, the Chinese ambassador to Thailand met the Secretary-General of the National Security Council (NSC). They are now concerned that the NSC may decide whether to return the two refugees to China in an upcoming meeting. They noted that a decision made by the NSC led to the deportation of 40 Uyghur refugees to China, and that none of the 40 refugees could be contacted to confirm their safety.
They call on the Thai government to stop the forced return to Uyghur refugees to China and to facilitate their resettlement in a third country in line with their wishes and that of the receiving country. The Thai government must allow legal representatives, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to access and protect the Uyghur refugees held in immigration detention. It must also respect the free and informed decisions of the two Uyghur refugees.

Prachinburi at risk of industrial waste contamination after flood
Pictures of oil-like scum on floodwater in Prachinburi have led to concerns of toxic contamination from industrial waste dumping sites in the area.
Oil-like scum floating on floodwaters in Prachinburi (Photo from EARTH Foundation)
On 29 September, the Ecological Alert and Recovery (EARTH) Thailand Foundation posted on its Facebook page that it had received pictures from locals in Prachinburi of oil-like scum on floodwaters covering rice fields in Prachinburi’s Si Maha Phot district. Locals said that the scum extends across waters flowing into the Si Mahosot district.
EARTH Foundation speculated that it may originate from an industrial waste landfill operated by Green Environment Technology company, which has a permit for waste sorting and landfill disposal. The company also has a permit for processing used lubricant and solvent, shredding electronic parts, and converting non-toxic waste into bricks.
Sumet Rianpongnam, an environmental activist from the Strong Prachinburi group, said that locals also informed his group about the scum. He said that chemicals and toxins were seeping out of the landfill before the flood. On 25 September, heavy rain caused a flood, and rainwater in the landfill overflowed, spreading toxic chemicals into rice fields.
“Oil was leaking before … but the problem has gotten worse with the flood. It now extends across thousands of rai … [and] we don‘t know how far the toxins will spread,“ said Sumet.
Observing that it depends on the flow of floodwaters, he expressed concern that as the water rises, more contamination could leak out of the site, which is now underwater.
The Strong Prachinburi group lodged a complaint with Prachinburi’s Provincial Industry Office on 28 September, according to EARTH Foundation. They have not received a response.
